content:
We have proton NMR data: peaks at 2.62 (t, J=7.3 Hz, 2H), 2.77 (t, J=7.3 Hz, 2H), aromatic region: 7.18 (ddd, 2H), 7.36 (ddd, 2H). So total protons: 2+2+2+2 = 8 H. Aromatic 4 H suggests a para-disubstituted benzene (AA'BB' pattern). Two aliphatic CH2 groups each 2H as triplets coupling to each other (J=7.3). Likely ethyl group attached to aromatic? But two CH2 groups both triplets suggests -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic on one end and something else on other end (maybe carbonyl). Could be phenylacetic acid? That has CH2 next to aromatic (singlet? Actually CH2 attached to aromatic appears as a singlet? No, phenylacetic acid: Ph-CH2-COOH, CH2 is a singlet because adjacent to carbonyl (no protons). Not matching.

We have two CH2 groups coupling to each other, both triplets, typical of -CH2-CH2- chain. So maybe para-disubstituted benzene with -CH2-CH2- substituents on each side? But total aromatic protons 4, so ring has two substituents para to each other. Each substituent could be -CH2-CH2- something. The aliphatic protons total 4, so each substituent contributes CH2-CH2? That would be 4 CH2 groups total 8 H, but we only have 4 H aliphatic. So maybe only one side has ethyl chain, other side is something without protons (e.g., carbonyl). So para-substituted benzene with ethyl group on one side and carbonyl (e.g., COOH) on other. That would give aromatic 4 H, ethyl CH2-CH2 attached to aromatic? Ethyl attached directly to aromatic would be -CH2-CH3, not CH2-CH2. But we have two CH2, not CH3. So maybe -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic via O (i.e., ethoxy). Ethoxy group: -O-CH2-CH3 gives CH3 (triplet) and CH2 (quartet). Not matching.

Two CH2 triplets suggests -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic on one end and to something like -Cl? But the other end maybe attached to carbonyl (CH2-CO-). That would be CH2 next to carbonyl (alpha to carbonyl) appears as triplet if adjacent to CH2. So structure could be para-ethyl ester? Example: ethyl benzoate: Ph-COO-CH2-CH3. That gives aromatic 5 H (monosubstituted). Not match.

Para-disubstituted with ethyl chain on one side and carbonyl on other: 4-ethylbenzoyl? Actually 4-ethylbenzoyl chloride? Ethyl attached directly to ring (CH2-CH3) gives CH3 triplet, CH2 quartet. Not match.

Our aliphatic chemical shifts: 2.62 and 2.77 ppm, both relatively downfield (near 2.5-2.8) typical for CH2 adjacent to aromatic ring (benzylic) and CH2 adjacent to carbonyl (alpha to carbonyl). Benzylic CH2 appears around 2.3-2.9. Alpha carbonyl CH2 appears around 2.3-2.5. So plausible: one CH2 is benzylic (attached to aromatic), other is carbonyl-adjacent (attached to carbonyl). So structure: para-substituted benzene with -CH2-CO- (acetyl) on one side and -CH2-Ph on other? Wait.

Consider compound: phenylacetic acid (Ph-CH2-COOH) gives one CH2 benzylic (2.5) and COOH not CH2. Not match.

Consider 4-(2-oxoethyl)benzonitrile? Not.

Better: 4-(2-oxoethyl)phenyl acetate? Hmm.

We have two CH2 groups coupling to each other, so they are adjacent. So chain -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic at one end and carbonyl at other end: aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-? That would be phenylpropionyl? Actually phenylpropionic acid: Ph-CH2-CH2-COOH. That has aromatic 5 H (monosubstituted). Not match.

But para-disubstituted: maybe 4-(2-oxoethyl)phenyl? That is phenyl attached to CH2-CH2-CO-? Wait.

If aromatic is para-disubstituted, one substituent is -CH2-CH2-CO- (propionyl) and other substituent is something non-proton (e.g., -Cl). Aromatic protons would be 4. The chain CH2-CH2-CO- gives two CH2 triplets. That matches. So candidate: 4-(propionyl)chlorobenzene? Actually substituents: para-chlorophenyl with propionyl group? That would be 4-chlorobenzoyl? Wait.

Propionyl group attached to aromatic via carbonyl: -CO-CH2-CH3 gives CH3 triplet, CH2 quartet. Not our pattern.

Our pattern is aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO- (alkyl chain attached to aromatic via CH2, not via carbonyl). So substituent is -CH2-CH2-CO- (propionyl attached via alkyl). That is phenylpropionyl? Actually phenylpropyl carbonyl? The carbonyl is at terminal end, maybe as ester? Could be para-ethyl benzoate? No.

Let's think of molecule: 4-(2-oxoethyl)phenyl? That is phenyl-CH2-CO-? That's only one CH2.

Our data: two CH2 adjacent, both downfield ~2.6-2.8, typical for CH2 next to aromatic and CH2 next to carbonyl. So chain is -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic at one end, carbonyl at other. So overall substituent is -CH2-CH2-CO- (propionyl attached via alkyl). The carbonyl could be part of an amide, ester, acid, etc. If it's acid, we have -CH2-CH2-COOH. That would be 4-phenylbutyric acid? Actually phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOH is phenylacetic acid? No, phenylacetic acid is Ph-CH2-COOH (one CH2). Phenylpropionic acid is Ph-CH2-CH2-COOH (two CH2). That matches chain. Phenylpropionic acid is monosubstituted phenyl (5 aromatic H). Not match.

But if phenyl ring is para-disubstituted, maybe one substituent is -CH2-CH2-COOH and other is something like -Cl. Aromatic protons 4. So candidate: 4-(3-carboxypropyl)chlorobenzene? Actually -CH2-CH2-COOH attached via CH2 to ring (propionic acid side chain). That would be 4-(3-carboxypropyl)chlorobenzene? Wait the side chain is -CH2-CH2-COOH attached via CH2 to ring, that's 3-phenylpropionic acid (phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOH). That's monosubstituted. To make para-disubstituted, need another substituent on opposite para position, maybe a halogen.

Thus overall formula: C? Let's try to deduce molecular formula from NMR: aromatic 4 H, aliphatic 4 H, plus maybe other protons not observed (like OH). Could be carboxylic acid OH (broad). Not in data.

Thus plausible SMILES: Clc1ccc(cc1)CCCO? Actually chain: aromatic-CH2-CH2-COOH. So SMILES: Clc1ccc(cc1)CCCO? Wait need carbonyl: O=C(O)CCc1ccc(Cl)cc1? But chain attaches via CH2 to aromatic, so O=C(O)CCc1ccc(Cl)cc1? That is 4-chlorophenylpropionic acid (para-chloro). SMILES: O=C(O)CCc1ccc(Cl)cc1. Aromatic protons: 4 (para-chloro). Yes.

Check NMR: aromatic protons of para-chlorobenzene appear as AA'BB' doublets around 7.2-7.4. Good. Aliphatic CH2 next to aromatic (benzylic) ~2.7, CH2 next to carbonyl ~2.6. Both triplets J~7.3. Good.

Thus answer likely O=C(O)CCc1ccc(Cl)cc1.

Let's verify with search? Could use search_by_smiles to see if matches NMR.
